items.prompt: A workload consists of independent containerized jobs that can wait in a queue and should scale compute from zero. Which service should be evaluated?
constraints: The application uses containers or supported job definitions.

options.text: Evaluate AWS Batch with job queues, compute environments, instance or Fargate capacity, retries, and vCPU or resource requirements modeled.
Use a continuously running EC2 fleet sized for the maximum queue.
Use Lambda for jobs that exceed its duration or package limits.
Use CloudFront to schedule batch containers.

feedback.Reason: AWS Batch manages queued jobs and compute environments for scalable batch execution.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Batch separates job queues and definitions from compute environments that can scale supported capacity.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner defines resource requirements, priorities, retries, capacity type, and completion monitoring.
Details.errorCorrection: A max-sized fleet wastes capacity, Lambda has execution limits, and CloudFront is not a batch scheduler.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Queue-based execution trades immediate latency for efficient capacity and job control.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A permanent maximum fleet overprovisions idle capacity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Lambda may not fit duration, storage, or container requirements.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: CloudFront does not schedule compute jobs.

items.prompt: A Batch job needs privileged host access and a specialized EC2 instance family. Which compute environment should be compared?
constraints: The container needs host or instance capabilities.

options.text: Evaluate a managed EC2 compute environment, sizing instance type, allocation strategy, vCPU, memory, storage, and scaling behavior for the job.
Use Fargate because every container workload has identical host requirements.
Use Lambda because Batch jobs cannot use EC2.
Use a fixed bare-metal host without a queue or retry design.

feedback.Reason: Batch EC2 environments support instance-family and host capabilities that serverless container capacity may not.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Batch can use managed compute environments backed by EC2 or Fargate with different resource and operational boundaries.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect matches privileged, storage, network, and accelerator needs to an EC2 environment and job definition.
Details.errorCorrection: Fargate has a supported feature set, Lambda is a different model, and one host removes queue elasticity and recovery.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: EC2 offers control and family choice but adds instance capacity and AMI management.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Fargate does not expose every host capability or instance family.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Batch can run jobs on EC2 compute environments.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A fixed host does not provide managed queue scale or replacement.

items.prompt: A fault-tolerant Batch job can restart from checkpoints and needs the lowest compute cost. Which capacity type should be evaluated?
constraints: The workload is flexible about completion time.

options.text: Evaluate Spot capacity in a managed Batch compute environment with diversified instance types, retry, checkpoint, and interruption-aware job behavior.
Use Spot for a job that cannot restart or recover from interruption.
Disable retries because interruption means the data is invalid.
Use only one Spot instance type and Availability Zone for maximum resilience.

feedback.Reason: Spot fits interruptible batch work when the job and capacity strategy handle replacement.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Spot capacity can be interrupted and is best used with retries, diversification, checkpoints, and flexible deadlines.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner configures allocation and job retry behavior, stores checkpoints durably, and monitors queue age and interruption rate.
Details.errorCorrection: Non-restartable work is unsafe on Spot, disabling retries loses work, and one pool concentrates capacity risk.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Lower cost trades for interruption and possible queue delay.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A non-restartable job cannot tolerate Spot interruption.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Retries are part of the recovery design.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Diversification reduces but does not remove capacity interruption risk.

items.prompt: A Batch job is queued indefinitely because its requested memory and vCPU combination is unavailable. What should be reviewed?
constraints: The compute environment has finite instance shapes.
The queue has a completion objective.

options.text: Compare job resource requirements with available instance or task shapes, compute environment limits, quotas, and queue priority, then adjust the job or capacity deliberately.
Increase queue priority without checking whether any capacity can satisfy the shape.
Remove resource requests so the scheduler can guess safely.
Run the job on the smallest instance regardless of memory requirements.

feedback.Reason: Batch scheduling needs a feasible resource shape and capacity, not just priority.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Job definitions, compute environment instance types, quotas, and queue scheduling determine whether a job can start.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner tests a representative job, configures compatible types and headroom, and alarms on queue age.
Details.errorCorrection: Priority cannot create an infeasible shape, omitted resources risk failure, and undersizing causes OOM or poor performance.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Broader instance choices improve schedulability but can change cost and performance.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Priority does not fix incompatible resource requirements.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Schedulers need explicit resource requirements to place jobs safely.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Insufficient memory causes failure rather than efficient execution.

items.prompt: A workload runs the same container independently over thousands of input shards. Which Batch feature should be evaluated?
constraints: Failures can be retried per child job.

options.text: Evaluate an array job with per-child input assignment, resource requirements, retry behavior, result collection, and downstream fan-in modeled.
Run one huge job and store all shard state in local temporary storage.
Create a separate manually managed cluster for every shard.
Use one Lambda invocation with all shards in one payload regardless of limits.

feedback.Reason: Array jobs express many related independent child jobs with shared scheduling and retry semantics.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: AWS Batch array jobs create child jobs with indexed identities and can be combined with queue and resource controls.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner maps index to shard, persists results durably, retries failed children, and performs a controlled fan-in.
Details.errorCorrection: One huge job increases failure blast radius, manual clusters add operations, and Lambda payloads and duration are bounded.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Array orchestration simplifies scale but still requires limits, result aggregation, and idempotency.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: One job makes a single failure affect all shards.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Manual cluster-per-shard management is unnecessary overhead.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: One invocation can exceed Lambda payload, duration, or concurrency constraints.

items.prompt: An EMR cluster has a coordinator that needs memory and core nodes that need compute and storage throughput. What selection principle applies?

options.text: Select master, core, and task instance types from their distinct memory, CPU, storage, network, and failure roles, then validate workload scaling.
Use one instance type for every EMR node regardless of role.
Use the smallest master because it never affects cluster scheduling.
Use Spot for all critical core storage nodes without replication or interruption planning.

feedback.Reason: EMR node roles can have different resource and durability requirements.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: EMR separates primary, core, and task responsibilities; instance type and capacity affect coordination, storage, compute, and recovery.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect sizes each role, chooses task elasticity, and protects core data and cluster state from interruptions.
Details.errorCorrection: Uniform types can waste resources, an undersized primary can bottleneck orchestration, and critical core nodes need interruption planning.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Heterogeneous nodes improve fit but increase sizing and operational complexity.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Node roles have different resource profiles.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: The primary node can be a coordination bottleneck.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Core storage roles need a recovery and interruption-aware design.

items.prompt: An EMR Spark job has reproducible task work and durable input and output, but core nodes must remain stable. Which capacity design fits?

options.text: Evaluate Spot task nodes with stable core capacity, interruption-aware Spark configuration, and checkpoint or retry behavior.
Use Spot for all core nodes without modeling lost shuffle or storage state.
Use On-Demand task nodes only because task work cannot be retried.
Delete durable input after tasks begin to reduce storage cost.

feedback.Reason: EMR task nodes are often suitable for interruptible, recomputable work while core capacity holds cluster data and services.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: EMR instance fleets and groups can use Spot or On-Demand roles with different interruption and storage effects.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner preserves core capacity, configures task replacement and retries, and keeps durable input and output.
Details.errorCorrection: Core Spot interruption can affect storage and cluster stability, tasks can often retry, and deleting input is unsafe.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Spot lowers task compute cost but can increase completion time and rework.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Core nodes can hold state that is not equivalent to recomputable task work.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Task nodes can use Spot when the workload and retry model support it.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Durable input is required for retries and recovery.

items.prompt: An EMR cluster often cannot obtain one preferred instance type in a Region. Which capacity strategy should be evaluated?
constraints: The workload can run on several compatible types.
The job has a completion objective.

options.text: Use an instance fleet or diversified capacity strategy with compatible types and weighted resource units, validating performance and price across alternatives.
Require one exact type and retry indefinitely.
Mix incompatible architectures without testing the application image.
Use the cheapest type even if it cannot meet memory or storage requirements.

feedback.Reason: Diversification improves capacity availability when compatible instance types satisfy the workload.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: EMR instance fleets can request multiple instance types and capacity options with weighted requirements.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect defines compatibility, benchmarks alternatives, and monitors cluster resource and job performance.
Details.errorCorrection: One-type dependence causes launch failures, mixed architectures need compatible artifacts, and cheap but undersized capacity fails jobs.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Diversification improves launch probability but requires testing and can change cost or performance.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Exact-type dependence exposes availability and capacity risk.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Architecture mixing requires compatible images and binaries.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Price is not a substitute for resource fit.

items.prompt: An EMR Spark job spills heavily because executors lack memory, while CPU is not saturated. Which change should be evaluated?
constraints: The workload has shuffle or cache state.
The cluster can be resized or rebalanced.

options.text: Compare memory-optimized or larger worker types and Spark executor sizing, then validate shuffle, network, storage, and cost effects.
Add CPU-only nodes because spilling is always a CPU issue.
Increase S3 bucket size to provide executor memory.
Reduce memory allocation per executor without measuring spill or runtime.

feedback.Reason: EMR worker selection must follow the dominant resource and the framework's executor behavior.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Spark memory, executor count, shuffle, network, and local storage interact with the underlying instance profile.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner tunes worker family and executor layout from spill, GC, CPU, network, and job duration metrics.
Details.errorCorrection: CPU nodes do not add memory, S3 capacity is not executor RAM, and reducing memory can worsen spill.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: More memory can reduce spill but may lower CPU density or increase cost.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: CPU capacity does not solve insufficient executor memory.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Object storage capacity is not host memory.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Less memory can increase spill, GC, and duration.

items.prompt: An EMR job is CPU-bound with low memory use and high parallelism. Which worker family should be compared?
constraints: CPU is measured as the bottleneck.
Input and shuffle paths are provisioned.

options.text: Evaluate compute-optimized worker instances and validate executor count, network, local storage, shuffle, and cost per completed job.
Use high-memory nodes because every distributed job needs maximum RAM.
Use GPU nodes without accelerator-compatible algorithms.
Reduce worker count to lower CPU utilization without checking completion time.

feedback.Reason: Compute-optimized workers are candidates for CPU-bound distributed jobs when memory and data paths remain adequate.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: EMR worker family and size affect executor CPU, memory, network, local storage, and job parallelism.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect benchmarks job time and cost while checking that shuffle and input do not become the new bottleneck.
Details.errorCorrection: Memory-heavy nodes can waste cost, GPUs need algorithm support, and fewer workers can lengthen the job.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: More CPU density can improve job time but may need larger data paths and increases fleet cost.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Extra memory is not useful when CPU is the measured limit.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Accelerators require supported algorithms and frameworks.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Lower count can reduce cost but violate completion objectives.

items.prompt: An EMR job performs large local sequential shuffle and spill operations and needs high instance storage throughput. Which worker option should be evaluated?
constraints: Local storage is the measured bottleneck.
Data can be recomputed or protected.

options.text: Evaluate storage-optimized or local-NVMe worker types, validating capacity, throughput, loss behavior, shuffle configuration, and job recovery.
Use the smallest local disk because shuffle is always remote.
Use S3 as a transparent local filesystem for every spill operation.
Use instance store as durable output without exporting results.

feedback.Reason: Local storage-intensive EMR workloads need workers with suitable disk throughput and an explicit ephemeral-data model.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Some EC2 families provide local NVMe or storage density; shuffle and spill behavior depend on framework and node layout.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner benchmarks spill, disk queueing, network, and recovery and keeps durable output outside ephemeral disks.
Details.errorCorrection: Shuffle can use local storage, S3 is not transparent local disk, and instance store output can be lost.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Local storage improves performance but adds capacity and node-replacement considerations.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Local spill can be a major performance path.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: S3 access has different latency and filesystem semantics.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Ephemeral local storage is not durable output storage.

items.prompt: An EMR workload has variable hourly input and the cluster is idle between jobs. What scaling design should be considered?

options.text: Evaluate managed or application-driven EMR scaling with minimum and maximum capacity, metric selection, bootstrap time, queue age, and graceful scale-in behavior.
Keep maximum capacity running because autoscaling always increases job cost.
Scale only on CPU without considering YARN or job backlog.
Terminate core nodes immediately when CPU falls below a threshold.

feedback.Reason: EMR scaling must follow workload backlog and resource pressure while protecting cluster state and job completion.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: EMR managed scaling uses cluster and workload metrics to adjust capacity within configured bounds.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner chooses minimum core capacity, scales task or worker resources from queue and utilization signals, and validates scale-in.
Details.errorCorrection: Permanent maximum capacity wastes idle time, CPU alone can miss queue pressure, and core termination can lose state.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Scaling reduces idle cost but adds warm-up delay and can disrupt work if thresholds are wrong.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Keeping maximum capacity can increase idle cost.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: CPU alone may not represent queued work or memory pressure.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Core nodes can contain important cluster data and need graceful handling.

items.prompt: A scheduled EMR job runs once per day and has no interactive users between runs. What lifecycle choice should be compared?
constraints: Data is durable outside the cluster.

options.text: Evaluate transient clusters created for the job and terminated after success, with reproducible configuration, durable input and output, and failure cleanup.
Keep the cluster running indefinitely even when idle.
Store the only job output on local cluster disks before termination.
Create a new cluster manually with undocumented settings every day.

feedback.Reason: Transient EMR clusters fit scheduled workloads when data and configuration are externalized.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: EMR clusters can be created for a workload and terminated, while S3 or other durable services hold data and artifacts.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner automates creation, bootstrap, logs, retries, output validation, and termination on success or failure.
Details.errorCorrection: Idle clusters cost money, local disks are ephemeral, and manual undocumented creation is not reproducible.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Cluster startup adds latency, so it must fit the job schedule and RTO.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: An idle persistent cluster adds avoidable compute cost.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Local disks are not a durable output repository.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Manual drift increases failure and recovery risk.

items.prompt: An EMR cluster starts but jobs fail because required libraries are absent. What design improvement is needed?
constraints: The cluster is recreated or scaled.

options.text: Use versioned bootstrap actions, custom images or configuration where appropriate, validate dependency installation during provisioning, and fail clearly before job submission.
Install dependencies manually after each cluster launches.
Assume task nodes inherit every package from the primary node automatically.
Ignore dependency failures until the job reaches production data.

feedback.Reason: Reproducible EMR provisioning is required for transient and scaling clusters.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Bootstrap actions and cluster configuration install packages and settings on nodes during creation.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner versions the configuration, tests new nodes, records logs, and blocks job submission on provisioning failure.
Details.errorCorrection: Manual installation causes drift, node packages are not implicitly identical, and late failure wastes compute and window.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Custom provisioning adds build and test work but makes recovery and scaling repeatable.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Manual setup is slow and non-reproducible.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Node role and provisioning behavior must be configured explicitly.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Late discovery increases failure blast radius and cost.

items.prompt: An EMR cluster has idle CPU but a growing YARN queue because memory is exhausted. Which scaling signal is correct?

options.text: Scale or resize from YARN resource pressure and queue age, not CPU alone, while validating memory, executor placement, and scale-in behavior.
Do nothing because idle CPU proves the cluster has spare capacity.
Add CPU-only instances that do not add schedulable memory.
Kill queued jobs to reduce queue age without changing capacity.

feedback.Reason: Cluster capacity is multidimensional and YARN memory pressure can coexist with idle CPU.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: YARN schedules resources such as memory and vcores; queue age and pending resources reveal the limiting dimension.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner chooses compatible worker sizes, monitors queue and executor metrics, and avoids scale-in that disrupts active work.
Details.errorCorrection: Idle CPU does not mean schedulable memory, CPU-only nodes do not fix memory, and killing jobs hides the problem.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Adding memory may bring unused CPU, so the family ratio should be tested.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Another resource can be exhausted while CPU is idle.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Nodes must provide the resource YARN cannot schedule.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Deleting work is not capacity management.

items.prompt: An EMR job reads a large dataset and spends most of its time transferring data from a distant repository. Which compute review is appropriate?
constraints: Data transfer is the measured bottleneck.
The job has a fixed completion window.

options.text: Evaluate data locality, S3 or source layout, cluster placement, network bandwidth, input format, compression, and worker count before simply adding CPU.
Add CPU until network transfer becomes faster automatically.
Move the cluster to a random Region without data-residency or latency review.
Use an instance type with less network bandwidth to reduce cost while keeping the same deadline.

feedback.Reason: Distributed compute performance can be dominated by data movement rather than worker CPU.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Input placement, object layout, compression, network path, and worker bandwidth determine data ingestion rate.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect co-locates where appropriate, optimizes format and partitions, and scales the real bottleneck.
Details.errorCorrection: CPU does not increase a finite network path, random Region changes can violate requirements, and less bandwidth worsens transfer.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Staging or local caching costs storage and setup but can reduce job duration and compute waste.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: CPU cannot remove a network or data-locality bottleneck.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Region choice requires data and service analysis.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Lower network capacity conflicts with the fixed completion window.

items.prompt: A long EMR job can run for hours and must resume after cluster or task failure. What compute design is required?

options.text: Write checkpoints and intermediate state to durable storage, configure retry or step recovery, and size cluster replacement and restart time against the RTO.
Keep the only checkpoint on local instance storage because it is fastest.
Disable retries so the cluster never repeats work.
Increase worker count without adding any durable checkpoint path.

feedback.Reason: Long distributed jobs need durable progress and a measured recovery path.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Cluster and instance failures can remove local state; durable checkpoints and repeatable steps reduce restart work.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner tests failure injection, checkpoint frequency, replacement capacity, and output consistency.
Details.errorCorrection: Local instance storage is ephemeral, disabling retries loses progress, and more workers do not create recovery state.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Frequent checkpoints add I/O and duration but reduce recovery work and data loss.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Local instance state can be lost with the node.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: No retry means a transient failure becomes a job failure.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Compute capacity does not substitute for durable progress.

items.prompt: A Batch job fails because a downstream API throttles during parallel execution. What should be changed?

options.text: Bound Batch concurrency or job arrays, add retry backoff, protect the downstream quota, and monitor queue age and failure reason.
Increase parallelism so the API recovers faster.
Retry immediately without a maximum attempt count.
Remove the downstream call and mark the job successful without data validation.

feedback.Reason: Batch parallelism must respect downstream quotas and use bounded retry behavior.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Job queues can generate concurrent calls that exceed external service limits; retry and concurrency settings shape pressure.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner sets a safe fan-out, uses backoff, sends permanent failures to a visible path, and validates results.
Details.errorCorrection: More parallelism worsens throttling, unbounded retry amplifies load, and skipping work creates incorrect output.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Lower concurrency can lengthen completion time but preserves downstream availability.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Parallelism above the dependency quota worsens throttling.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Unbounded retries can create a retry storm.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Marking failed work successful violates correctness.

items.prompt: A team changes the EMR release and instance architecture together and the job fails during bootstrap. What is the safer rollout?
constraints: The job has a production deadline.

options.text: Test the release, runtime, architecture, bootstrap, and application dependencies separately where possible, then canary the combined change with rollback.
Change all dimensions simultaneously because one failure has one obvious cause.
Keep the old release forever without reviewing support or security.
Skip testing because EMR manages the control plane.

feedback.Reason: EMR release and instance choices form a compatibility contract that needs controlled testing.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Framework release, AMI, architecture, bootstrap, and application dependencies interact during cluster creation and job execution.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner uses a representative test, records output and performance, and keeps a known-good release or image for rollback.
Details.errorCorrection: Changing everything obscures root cause, indefinite old releases create support risk, and managed control plane does not validate the job.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Canary testing adds time but limits production failure blast radius.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Bundling changes makes failure diagnosis and rollback harder.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Old versions can lose support and security updates.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Managed service ownership does not cover application compatibility.

items.prompt: An EMR job misses its completion window, but the team has only cluster CPU graphs. Which observability gap matters?
constraints: The job framework exposes stage metrics.
Input, shuffle, and output are measurable.

options.text: Correlate job stage duration, executor or task failure, memory and GC, shuffle, disk, network, queue, input, and output metrics with cluster capacity.
Increase every node size without identifying the slow stage.
Monitor only cluster uptime.
Use final job success as the only performance signal.

feedback.Reason: A distributed job can be bottlenecked by stages, memory, shuffle, disk, network, or scheduling rather than aggregate CPU.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Framework-level metrics connect resource pressure to the stage and task causing the completion delay.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner traces the slow stage, changes worker ratio or data layout, and verifies job duration and cost.
Details.errorCorrection: Blind scale-up can waste cost, uptime says nothing about completion, and final success is too late for an SLO.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Deep telemetry costs storage and tooling but makes compute sizing evidence-based.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Larger nodes may not fix a data, shuffle, or scheduling bottleneck.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Uptime does not measure job completion performance.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Final success cannot explain missed deadlines or tail behavior.

items.prompt: A Batch queue has a strict completion deadline and compute environments scale from zero. Which headroom calculation is needed?

options.text: Include queue age, provisioning and bootstrap time, job duration, capacity availability, retries, and failure recovery in the required headroom calculation.
Size only for average job count and ignore startup or retry time.
Set maximum capacity to zero because Batch can always launch just in time.
Increase job timeout to guarantee deadline completion.

feedback.Reason: Batch deadline capacity includes provisioning delay and recovery, not just average execution demand.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Compute environments need time and capacity to launch; queue, retries, and interruptions consume the completion window.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner keeps warm or reserved capacity when needed and measures queue-to-completion against the deadline.
Details.errorCorrection: Average demand hides peaks and launch delay, zero capacity adds startup risk, and timeout does not create compute.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Warm capacity costs more but protects a hard completion objective.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Startup and retry time can dominate a fixed deadline.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Scale-from-zero is not instantaneous or guaranteed.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Timeout only changes failure timing, not capacity availability.

items.prompt: A review compares AWS Batch, EMR, Lambda, and a persistent EC2 cluster for data processing. What selection method is correct?
constraints: Job duration and dependency graph are known.
Data locality and framework are explicit.

options.text: Map framework and execution model, job duration, resource shape, queue or interactive latency, data movement, elasticity, failure handling, and operational ownership to one service.
Choose the service with the most vCPUs regardless of job semantics.
Choose Lambda for all jobs because it has no servers to manage.
Choose a persistent cluster because batch services cannot scale.

feedback.Reason: Batch, EMR, Lambda, and persistent EC2 solve different execution and data-processing contracts.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Service limits, framework support, scheduling, resource shapes, data locality, and operations differ across compute models.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect selects the simplest fit and validates performance, cost, retry, observability, and recovery.
Details.errorCorrection: vCPU count ignores semantics, Lambda has hard limits, and managed batch services can scale capacity.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A managed service reduces operations but may constrain framework, placement, or runtime behavior.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Raw capacity does not determine execution-model fit.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Lambda is bounded by duration, payload, concurrency, and runtime behavior.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Batch and EMR are designed to scale managed compute for suitable workloads.
